players.product: solid-oxide fuel cells for data-center onsite power

quarterly_data.signal: Q3 2026 results (CFO Simon Edwards, non-GAAP), 'another record quarter': revenue of $1.24 billion, up 138% year over year and 16% sequentially; product revenue $1.07 billion, up 179% year over year and 15% sequentially, crossing $1 billion in a quarter for the first time and 87% of total revenue; service revenue $67.6 million, up 15%; installation revenue $84.9 million, up 29% year over year and 66% sequentially. Product gross margin 38.4%, up 250 basis points year over year, 'in a quarter when we were both ramping new production lines and expediting deliveries'; services margin 21.4%, up 700 basis points, the second consecutive quarter above 20%; total gross margin 34.5%, up 412 basis points. Operating expenses $141 million (up only 26% while revenue grew 138%); operating income $286 million, up over 500% year over year and 19% sequentially, exceeding operating income for all of last year; operating margin 23.1% versus 8.9% a year ago; adjusted EBITDA $299 million (24% of revenue). Non-GAAP diluted EPS 94 cents versus 15 cents a year ago; GAAP diluted EPS 78 cents. Year-to-date revenue of $3.05 billion is already 50% above all of 2025.
quarterly_data.figure: Revenue $1.24 billion (+138% YoY); product revenue $1.07 billion (+179%); gross margin 34.5%; operating income $286 million; operating margin 23.1%; non-GAAP EPS 94 cents

quarterly_data.signal: FY2026 outlook raised for the third time this year (CFO Simon Edwards): revenue $4.4 to $4.6 billion, year-over-year growth of approximately 122% at the midpoint, reflecting Q3 performance and 'greater visibility into fourth quarter customer delivery timing'; the outlook is built on backlog assessed customer-by-customer against site readiness plus a probability-weighted view of the pipeline, and 'the timing of a small number of deliveries around year-end will determine where in the range we land'. Non-GAAP gross margin outlook maintained at approximately 34% (30% in 2025; original 2026 outlook approximately 32%); non-GAAP operating income raised to $960 million to $1.03 billion, a 22% operating margin at the midpoint versus 14% at the midpoint of the February outlook; non-GAAP diluted EPS $3.10 to $3.40. CEO K.R. Sridhar: 'We started our 2026 Q1 earnings call expecting a year-on-year revenue growth of 60%.'
quarterly_data.figure: FY2026 revenue $4.4 to $4.6 billion (approximately 122% growth at midpoint); gross margin approximately 34%; operating income $960 million to $1.03 billion; EPS $3.10 to $3.40

quarterly_data.signal: AEP / Google carbon-capture project and backlog: CEO K.R. Sridhar said 'AEP revealed that 700 megawatts of carbon capture and sequestration-enabled Bloom Energy servers will be used to provide Google with near net zero electricity in a first-of-its-kind project', Asked about the largest single-site deployment, the CEO said 'we are in the 100 megawatt class already. And the Wyoming is also a 100 megawatt class approaching the gigawatt class because 700 megawatts', and 'our largest systems are approaching the gigawatt scale' while the smallest are 150 kilowatts. CEO: 'Our customer pipeline continues to grow, and our backlog is continuing to expand faster than our revenue', with increasing diversity in customers, verticals and geographies. Asked about backlog growth, management said exact numbers come with the Q4 report and 'expect a solid growth'.
quarterly_data.figure: 700 megawatts of CCS-enabled Bloom Energy servers (AEP project for Google); backlog expanding faster than revenue

quarterly_data.signal: Manufacturing capacity and capex: CEO K.R. Sridhar on the decision to expand the Fremont real-estate footprint: 'the 5 gigawatt milestone which was just a milestone in a long journey we can clearly see that coming, and we need to get prepared for what is after that'; capacity is added like 'an analog dial', never in a step function, 'we will never be slow enough where we are the bottleneck to our customer getting the power', with no timeline given. Management on pace: 'We have not given any numbers on quarter to quarter growth or year growth'; 'I don't see us dialing down anytime soon. It's all dialing up.' CFO Simon Edwards: capex was $153 million in the quarter and $231 million year to date (four times what was spent in all of 2025), 'driven primarily by investments in machinery and production capacity to support expansion, within our existing Fremont and Newark facilities'; working capital rose with inventory built for future deliveries. CEO on productivity, relaying a line of the factory's general manager: at 100 megawatts a year of stack production Bloom had about 600 employees, at a gigawatt production it will have 600 employees in that production line, 'And when we get to 5 gigawatts, we'll still have 600 employees working in that line'.
quarterly_data.figure: capex $153 million in Q3, $231 million year to date; preparing for capacity beyond 5 gigawatts

quarterly_data.signal: Market expansion (CEO K.R. Sridhar): the value proposition 'has become competitive even in the American states with the lowest cost of power. Such as Texas. Where we are shipping our first units this quarter', with an expanding footprint in the Rocky Mountain, Midwest and Great Lakes regions. Internationally Bloom is 'witnessing strong interest' and is 'engaged with potential local partners in a few of these markets', adding 'expect some good news from us in the near future'; higher natural-gas costs abroad 'even further' enhance its advantage. Utilities: he expects 'significant wins in our utility-related business, often called "front of the meter" arrangements', as utilities 'are finally getting the leeway they need from their regulators to include these assets', which he calls 'a huge growth business for us going forward'.
quarterly_data.figure: first units shipping in Texas this quarter

quarterly_data.signal: U.S. Army win (CEO K.R. Sridhar): 'the U.S. Army has conditionally awarded our partner indelible long-term leases to build and operate commercial power generation using Bloom Energy servers at U.S. Army installations', to enhance power security; Bloom views securely powering military and civilian critical infrastructure such as bases, water treatment plants, hospitals and airports as a growth opportunity.

Cash and working capital (CFO Simon Edwards): cash flow from operations was a use of $27 million as working capital rose (inventory, contract assets, receivables); free cash flow was a use of $181 million in the quarter and positive $42 million year to date; the quarter ended with $2.5 billion of cash, roughly in line with the start of the year. CFO: this quarter's operating cash use is 'not the beginning of a trend'; 'we already view this as a self-funding business' and 'we really do believe that this business will be a free cash flow positive business'. On contract assets (management, in Q&A): balances may grow but 'what's really important for us is that they're turning because we're reaching those billing milestones and we're collecting cash'.
quarterly_data.figure: operating cash flow -$27 million; free cash flow -$181 million in Q3, +$42 million year to date; cash $2.5 billion

quarterly_data.signal: Gross margin trajectory (CFO Simon Edwards): total gross margin was 28.7% in 2024, 30.3% in 2025 and 34.5% in Q3 2026; 'pricing remains strong' and cost reductions are 'showing up in the numbers', but ramping new production lines and expediting deliveries 'carries some near-term cost', and engineering, sourcing and manufacturing cost-reduction programs 'will take some time to flow through to COGS'; the full-year outlook stays measured, and 'as we continue to mature our lines and utilization increases, we think we'll get more benefit from scale'.

Platform options - carbon capture, 800V DC, CHP (CEO K.R. Sridhar): Bloom's technology 'is unique in that it can offer the concentrated carbon dioxide for carbon capture', and he sees carbon capture as 'a greater-than-a-trillion-dollar opportunity' 'when the world is ready'. Management: 'there is significant interest from all our hyperscale customers today asking about the optionality of carbon capture', 'I think almost all our customers would very soon at a minimum start buying systems from us that are carbon capture ready'; 'think about a 10 to 15 percent cost as being a reasonable cost that most hyperscalers today would accept' for zero-carbon power, and Bloom 'will be able to deliver in that range all in full cost for carbon capture and sequestration'. Monetisation can be through server sales, a partner offering an end-to-end solution, or a customer keeping the credits - 'We are agnostic to all of them'. On 800V DC: 'We are in conversations with all the hyperscalers', adoption will happen 'when the server racks with 800-volt DC come out' - 'It is not if. It is how soon.' On heat capture (CHP), using waste heat for cooling can reduce '20% of your power demand', which he sees as a large growth vector for commercial and industrial customers.
quarterly_data.figure: carbon capture seen as a greater-than-a-trillion-dollar opportunity; 10 to 15 percent cost hyperscalers would accept for zero-carbon power

quarterly_data.signal: Market view (CEO K.R. Sridhar): hyperscalers were the first to embrace on-site power, and 'Bloom quickly emerged as a standard solution'; Bloom's own power survey of over 200 commercial and industrial businesses found one quarter of U.S. commercial and industrial facilities expect to be fully powered on-site by 2030 and 35% by 2035; he expects the electricity market to grow annually to about $6 trillion in the next decade from about $3 trillion today, with Bloom 'a leader' in capturing it. On water, he said a wet-cooled combined-cycle gas plant for a 1 gigawatt data center would consume 'somewhere in the neighborhood of 25,000 million gallons' over its life, against 1.4 million for Bloom. He argued the relevant cost is the electricity cost per token delivered, not LCOE, on which Bloom is 'the overwhelming cost leader'. On time to power, he said the revenue a data center loses to a quarter's delay 'overwhelms every other value proposition that you will have on the power block'.
quarterly_data.figure: electricity market about $6 trillion in the next decade vs about $3 trillion today; survey: one quarter of U.S. C&I facilities fully on-site by 2030, 35% by 2035
